episode_title: MORE Stories That Should be Films

stories.summary: The pitch began with a dream. The show's cinematographer, Vaishnav Vyas, dreamt that Ajay was stealing everyone's paperwork, and Amit turned that into a quiet love story. The hero is a geeky, unmarried man in his early fifties. He lives in a messy flat full of wires, storage boxes and Maggi packets, in an oldish building that could be in Bandra East. He picks up his neighbours' electricity bills from their doorsteps. Residents with no bill in hand forget to pay, and his friend in the electricity department cuts their power. Then the helpful 'Ajay Bhai' gets it reconnected for the bill amount, a late fee and a bribe, and the two split the money. The habit grew out of a hoarder's compulsion: he sees paper and can't help collecting it. A woman in her forties moves in alone, and her bill vanishes too, but she never comes to him because she is too ill to get out of bed. He is moved, gets her power back and offers to make her dal chawal. He botches it and gets it from somewhere else, and as she eats she quietly realises he couldn't have cooked it. She cooks for him in return, and we see her obsessive-compulsive neatness. At his place she tries to shut a bathroom cupboard that keeps springing open and finds his hoard of bills, including her own. She storms out threatening to call the police, but never reports him. In the end she sees he meant no real harm, since the money funded his electronics hobby, and he apologises clumsily. The final shot: doorbells ring across the building, doors open in split-screen, every bill is there, and the residents dance over the credits.
stories.insight: Amit makes a petty rent-seeker sympathetic, a small human version of the 'hafta' state. He also shows the screenwriter's craft: the wires, the Maggi, the dip-dip tea and her tidiness are each planted early so they pay off later, without a line of explanation.
stories.quote: You would have thought that this is an evil grifter, he's taking advantage of others, but no. He is human. He is touched by this.

stories.topic: The Khalsa Bridge: Bota Singh and Garja Singh, 1739
stories.summary: Amit takes this from Sarbpreet Singh's history of the Sikhs, and the date is 27 July 1739. Zakaria Khan governs Punjab for the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah, and he has crushed a Sikh revolt so thoroughly that the Sikhs are in hiding. Two young Sikhs, Bota Singh and Garja Singh, are hiding in the fields when they overhear a farmer sneer that they aren't lions ('singh') but jackals, because real lions don't run and hide. Stung, they 'conquer' an empty wooden bridge beside a sarai on the Delhi–Lahore road. They then levy a 'Khalsa regime tax' of one paisa per donkey and six per cart. Every traveller simply pays. Garja is happy with the money, but Bota says they came to be warriors, not traders. Wanting a real fight, Bota sends Zakaria Khan a taunting verse letter that addresses him as 'sister-in-law'. With no war on, the governor is bored and rides out himself with a hundred horses. In the Sikh accounts, the two beat back wave after wave until the Mughals use guns and shoot them in the legs. With one working leg between them, they lock arms, face opposite directions and fight on until they die. Amit invents only their inner lives: Bota as his family's black sheep, Garja as a rejected suitor, both desperate for respect.
stories.insight: This is a story of alienation in the vein of Beckett and Stoppard. Two young men don't know what they want, so they die trying to prove something to others and to themselves. Amit turns it into a question for all of us about the futile battles we fight.
stories.quote: Are we standing on one leg against the power of the state, I ask you, against the power of bad ideas? We shall continue to stand, it is all we can do.

stories.topic: Two Chess Stories: Sultan Khan Meets Mr. B
stories.summary: Amit combines Stefan Zweig's novella The Royal Game with the real life of Sultan Khan. In Zweig's story, the mysterious Mr. B is held by the Nazis in solitary confinement with nothing but a chess book. He memorises its games, creates an alter ego and plays against himself again and again. Later, on a ship, he takes on a brilliant but uncultured world champion. Sultan Khan was born in 1903. He first became the best player of Indian chess, which has slightly different rules, and then learned European chess. He never read chess books or discussed the game with other players, yet he won the British Chess Championship in 1928 and won it three times in all. Then he returned to India and never played again. In Amit's fiction, Sultan's father is the family's black sheep, and the boy's wins over his father and then over the head of the household restore the father's standing. From then on every game becomes a fight for respect: his own, his family's, his nation's. Mr. B is a calculator who sees concrete lines far ahead. Sultan is an intuitive positional player who can picture the endgame pawn structure on move eight. The fictional Sultan becomes world champion and faces Mr. B in a reversed version of Zweig's match. He chooses to let Mr. B win.
stories.insight: Here chess is a means of finding out who you are. The real contest is the one inside each player's head, and seeing that clearly can mean letting go of the win.
stories.quote: he recognizes that the game that he has been playing all his life is not the game on the board. It is another game

stories.summary: Amit admits he likes to boast that he once beat a grandmaster. The fine print: he was 17, and his opponent was Abhijit Kunte, then a 14-year-old prodigy at a chess club on Karve Road in Pune and not yet a grandmaster. Kunte later became a grandmaster, Indian champion and British champion. Amit won one blitz game with a queen sacrifice, and the boy said, 'My God, I didn't know you could play like this.' They must have played dozens of blitz games, and Amit says he surely lost all the others.
stories.insight: A funny example of how a technically true claim can mislead by what it leaves out. It also captures how sweet it is to win just once against someone much better.
stories.quote: It is sweet joy to win even once.

stories.summary: In the 19th century the US post office built a public good: universal parcel delivery anywhere in the country at modest prices. People mailed potatoes and sacks of wheat. Then, almost as a joke, someone asked to post a child. The clerks played along. They weighed the child, charged the parcel rate and pasted the address on his shirt. The child was routed from one clearing centre to the next like any parcel and delivered, Ajay thinks, to his grandparents. It was talked about everywhere, and posting children became a normal thing, with postal employees feeding them along the way. Amit adds the human drama. A drunk father posts his surly, unloved son on a pub bet. A storm strands the boy for days in a sorting office, where a lonely old man, abandoned by his own grown children, bonds with the 'parcel' before it has to be sent on its way.
stories.insight: An absurd quirk of a real institution can reveal how much a society trusts strangers. Reality really can be stranger than fiction.
stories.quote: So they weighed the child and worked out the correct charges for the packet, and they said done.

recommendations.creator: Samuel Beckett
recommendations.context: Amit opens the Bota Singh and Garja Singh story by asking Ajay if he has seen or read this play.
recommendations.reason: The conversations between its two characters, Vladimir and Estragon, capture the alienation Amit wants for his two young Sikhs.

recommendations.creator: Tom Stoppard
recommendations.context: Amit's second model for the Khalsa Bridge story.
recommendations.reason: Stoppard takes two of Hamlet's friends, Shakespeare's minor characters, and builds a play 'a little bit about alienation' around them, which is the template for Amit's pair.

recommendations.item: Cauldron, Sword and Victory: The Rise of the Sikhs
recommendations.creator: Sarbpreet Singh
recommendations.context: Amit's source for the Bota Singh and Garja Singh episode, including the English translation of Bota Singh's letter to Zakaria Khan.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a 'magnificent' and 'excellent' book. He says it tells the complicated history of the Sikh rebellions against Mughal Punjab very well.

recommendations.item: Sarbpreet Singh Finds His Sikhism (Episode 407 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions recording with Sarbpreet Singh while crediting his book. He wasn't sure whether it would be out before this episode.
recommendations.reason: A chance to hear at length from the historian behind the Khalsa Bridge story.

recommendations.item: The Royal Game (also published as Chess Story)
recommendations.creator: Stefan Zweig
recommendations.context: Half of Amit's chess film. A Nazi prisoner who learned chess alone in solitary confinement takes on the world champion aboard a ship.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great novella and a very moving story. He has recommended it on the show before and suggests it may deserve an episode of its own.

recommendations.item: The Tamilian gentleman who took on the world
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's ESPN piece on Viswanathan Anand, brought up while discussing Sultan Khan.
recommendations.reason: It argues that Anand, without the Soviet school's systematic training, was like someone taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race. Sultan Khan faced the same situation decades earlier.

recommendations.creator: Adriaan de Groot
recommendations.context: De Groot's study of how far club players and experts think ahead, cited when Amit contrasts Mr. B's calculation with Sultan Khan's intuition.
recommendations.reason: Its finding is that grandmasters and novices look ahead the same number of moves. What sets grandmasters apart is pattern recognition.

recommendations.reason: The first episode in the series this one continues. Amit invites any listener who wants to produce one of these films to get in touch.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit explains Anton Chekhov's principle that nothing in a story should be there without a reason. He then shows it at work in his own pitch. The hero's tangle of wires sets up his geeky hoarding, his Maggi-and-dip-dip-tea kitchen sets up the failed dal chawal, and her obsessive neatness sets up the cupboard door she can't leave half-open.
core_ideas.quote: if you show a gun in the first act of the play, it must go off by the third act. Right? It should not be there for no reason.

core_ideas.concept: Show, Don't Spell Out the Why
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay suggests grounding the bill collector in the Marxist idea of alienation. Amit pushes back: the 'why' should come through in how characters live and act, not be stated outright. In his pitch the hero's isolation is told through the messy flat, and the woman realises he didn't cook the dal through a shared look.
core_ideas.quote: I think a mistake that mainstream films often make is they try to locate the why.

core_ideas.explanation: Both of Amit's first two stories are small studies of rent-seeking. The bill collector creates a problem and then charges to solve it, which Amit calls a mirror of the Indian state. On the bridge, Bota tells Garja they aren't traders, because nobody pays them voluntarily. They are 'like crooks or government', which to Bota mean the same thing. Amit notes that rent-seeking usually needs the state's connivance, but here travellers' apathy was enough: nobody asked who these two were, and the toll simply became normal.
core_ideas.quote: The bugger lied. The bugger is a thief. The bugger is everything we hate about the Indian state because this is what it is, basically, right? Rent seeking, hafta

core_ideas.explanation: History is usually written by the winners. Yet the only surviving accounts of the Khalsa Bridge come from the side that lost, in Sikh texts that treat the two men's deaths as martyrdom and a moral victory. That is why the fight reads like a superhero film. Narrative battles are old too: after an earlier clash, the Mughals and the Sikhs each claimed to have won.
core_ideas.quote: What is curious is that history is normally told from the winner's side. In this case, the only recountings we have of this event is from the loser's side

core_ideas.explanation: Adriaan de Groot found that strong and weak players look about equally far ahead. Expertise is mostly pattern recognition, though some players also calculate unusually well. Amit's two players stand for the two routes to mastery. Mr. B, trained by endlessly playing himself in a cell, calculates almost like an engine. Sultan Khan, self-taught and without a chess school, works by intuition about space, initiative and pawn structure.
core_ideas.quote: actually grandmasters and novices will think the same number of moves ahead. The grandmasters are better at pattern recognition.

core_ideas.explanation: This thread runs through Amit's stories. Bota and Garja die proving they aren't jackals. Sultan Khan has to win every game because his father's, his family's and his nation's pride depend on it. Amit asks how much of life is spent proving things to others and to ourselves, and whether the battle we are really fighting is the one in front of us at all.
core_ideas.quote: So many lives are lost because you're anxious to prove things to others, because you're anxious to prove things to yourself.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's takeaway from children being posted in America. Parents, postal workers and the children themselves all trusted strangers to behave well, enough to send a child across the country as a parcel. That level of social trust is a form of capital, and seen with today's eyes it is astonishing. Ajay also flags, and leaves for another day, why universal delivery was a public good rather than something markets supplied.
core_ideas.quote: It speaks very well for the trust capital of that country. That parents and post office employees and the kids were all comfortable with trusting in the good behavior of strangers.

core_ideas.concept: Two Ways to Pitch a Story
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay describes his approach as the opposite of Amit's. He looks for a striking real situation, sets out its rules, and leaves the human drama to someone else. Amit starts from inner lives: backstory, motive, glances and props. The postal-boy segment shows both, with Ajay's historical premise and Amit's improvised lonely old man.
core_ideas.quote: I think of it like setting up the rules of a situation. And then we require a genius like you to animate it with people and desires and all the human drama that I sort of leave as an exercise to the reader.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's response to the premise of a man stealing his neighbours' bills: 'If I would scoop up the bills of people, the only earthly reason would be to create a data set about electricity consumption.'
On casting: Vaishnav offered to play the Ajay-like hero, but Amit told him 'you're too young and handsome. Which is not to say you are not handsome, but you are not young.'
The cupboard door the obsessive-compulsive neighbour can't get shut 'springs back out like an adamant economist,' and when pushed again, 'springs back out further like a recalcitrant communist.'

Amit on male haplessness. Having offered to cook, the hero 'remembers that like all men he has overpromised.' When caught with the bills, he says 'I can explain': 'Have you ever been in a fight with a woman, Ajay Shah, where you have said something like I can explain, knowing that you can't? You have. An essential part of the human experience.'
Asked how he opens a wine bottle, Ajay says: 'Oh, there have been many disasters because there is no cork opener in my house.'
Amit refuses to reveal how the bill story resolves, saying audiences are suckers 'for good storytelling, not just good stories', and admitting it is 'partly because I haven't thought of them yet.'
Breaking Bad: Amit says the crew, Nomsita and Vaishnav, think Ajay would be a perfect Walter White. He also notes that the show has a pivotal reveal in a toilet, like his bathroom-cupboard scene.
The closing-credits song would swap 'dil' for 'bill' in an existing Hindi song: 'Bill Hai Ki Maanta Nahin'. Vaishnav's suggestion was 'Chura Liya... Bill Ko'.
Garja Singh's nickname was Mota Singh: 'So I presume that in appearance at least he might have looked a little bit like me.'
Raking in tolls, Garja works out the bridge's NPV 'like a true Baniya, or if there is any Gujarati blood' — a dig at Ajay.

Why a governor who has faced fifty thousand horses rides out against two men on a bridge: 'There are no ongoing wars. Number two, there is no television, no internet, no mobile phone, no OTTs to watch. So Zakaria Khan is bored.' On his hundred horses: 'I am guessing that they were humans with those horses.'

Bota Singh's letter to Zakaria Khan, in Sarbpreet Singh's translation: 'Staff in hand on the road I stand, a penny an ass, sixpence a cart, this is a toll that I command. My sister-in-law, my dear Khan, a response does Bota Singh demand.' Amit admits he doesn't quite understand why 'sister-in-law' was the insult.

Amit calls the Sikh retelling of the bridge fight 'like a Rajinikanth film'. He also describes his heroes as 'two random chunnu-munnus, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, Vladimir and Estragon, Bota and Garja.'
When Garja asks what's wrong with being traders, Amit calls back to an earlier episode on the Indian idea of ahimsa: traders, not raiders.
AlphaZero: Mr. B trains by playing against himself 'in the glorious tradition of Alpha Zero... though with considerably less computing capacity.'
Ajay on chess matches with a psychological edge: 'In Fischer–Spassky there is a psychological aspect, in Gukesh–Ding. Some matches are more normal than others, but these matches stick out.'

Indians could still play the British Chess Championship after independence. As Amit remembers it, after RB Ramesh and then Abhijit Kunte won it around 2002, the organisers decided: 'Fuck it, these Indians are winning it, no more Indians.' Today, he says, the top ten would all be Indian.
Amit's posted boy, stranded in a sorting office by a storm: 'there is no protocol of who feeds a parcel because you know, you don't normally need to feed parcels.'

Amit's modern postal-boy story: a friend in Bangalore who couldn't get an Uber booked a Dunzo parcel delivery from his office. When the rider arrived, he said 'I am the parcel' and rode to his destination on the back of the scooter.
